question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.

 

LACONIC
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Terse.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Laconic (adjective) means using very few words; brief and to the point in speech or writing. (संक्षिप्तभाषी, कम बोलने वाला)
◦ Example: His laconic reply of "Not yet" ended the discussion.

 

• Terse carries the same sense — short, concise and free of unnecessary words. (संक्षिप्त)
◦ Example: The minister issued a terse statement of three lines.

 

• The word comes from Laconia, the region of ancient Greece around Sparta, whose people were famous for their extremely short replies.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Verbose (शब्दाडम्बरपूर्ण): using more words than necessary — the opposite of laconic.

 

• Option 2: Garrulous (बकबक करने वाला): excessively talkative about trivial matters — also an antonym.

 

• Option 4: Loquacious (वाचाल): very talkative — again an antonym.

 

NOTE

 

• Note the pattern: three options here mean talkative and only one means brief. Fix the meaning of the given word first, then eliminate every option that agrees with the majority sense.

 

• Other synonyms of laconic: succinct, pithy, curt, concise, brusque.

question:
Choose the correct meaning of the given idiom.

 

To carry coals to Newcastle
option_1: To supply something to a place where it is already plentiful
option_2: To undertake a long and dangerous journey
option_3: To trade goods at a heavy financial loss
option_4: To bear a heavy burden without any help
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. To supply something to a place where it is already plentiful.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "To carry coals to Newcastle" means to do something completely pointless or superfluous, because the thing being supplied is already available there in abundance. (उल्टे गंगा बहाना — व्यर्थ का काम करना)
◦ Example: Sending textbooks to a publisher's own library is like carrying coals to Newcastle.

 

• Newcastle upon Tyne in England was for centuries the country's greatest coal-exporting port, so taking coal there was the very picture of a wasted effort.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 describes a hazardous journey, for which the idiom would be "to sail close to the wind" or "to run the gauntlet".

 

• Option 3 refers to loss-making trade; the idiom carries no sense of financial loss.

 

• Option 4 describes shouldering a burden alone — nearer to "to carry the can".

 

NOTE

 

• Idioms of futile effort frequently asked in SSC: "To beat the air", "To flog a dead horse", "To plough the sands", "To cry over spilt milk" and "To hold a candle to the sun".

question:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.

 

EPHEMERAL
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Enduring.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Ephemeral (adjective) means lasting for a very short time; short-lived. (क्षणभंगुर, अल्पकालिक)
◦ Example: The fame won by a single viral video is usually ephemeral.

 

• Its true opposite is enduring — lasting over a long period; permanent. (चिरस्थायी)
◦ Example: Her enduring contribution to the field is still cited today.

 

• The word comes from Greek ephemeros, meaning "lasting only a day" — the same root gives us the insect mayfly (Ephemeroptera), which lives barely a day as an adult.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Transient (क्षणिक): lasting only briefly — a synonym.

 

• Option 3: Fleeting (क्षणभंगुर): passing swiftly — also a synonym.

 

• Option 4: Momentary (क्षणभर का): lasting for a moment — again a synonym.

 

NOTE

 

• Other antonyms of ephemeral: perennial, perpetual, abiding, everlasting, imperishable.

 

• Words with the same "-emer/hemer" idea of a day: ephemeris (a table of daily astronomical positions).

question: Identify the misspelt word from the given options.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Occurence.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct spelling is "Occurrence" — an incident or event; the fact of something happening. (घटना)
◦ Example: Power cuts are a daily occurrence in the area during summer.

 

• Spelling key: OC + CUR + RENCE. The word takes double "c" and double "r", and ends in "-ence", not "-ance". The second "r" is doubled because the stress in occur falls on the last syllable, so the consonant doubles before the suffix (occur → occurred, occurring, occurrence).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Liaison (संपर्क, तालमेल) — correctly spelt; note the unusual sequence "ai–i".

 

• Option 2: Maintenance (रखरखाव) — correctly spelt; note that the verb is maintain but the noun drops the "i" → mainten-ance.

 

• Option 4: Conscientious (कर्तव्यनिष्ठ) — correctly spelt; contains "scien" as in science.

 

NOTE

 

• Distinguish the endings carefully: -ence in occurrence, persistence, existence, independence; -ance in maintenance, resistance, appearance, perseverance.

question: Spot the correct spelling of the branch of science that studies the functioning of the nervous system.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Neurophysiology.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Neurophysiology" is the branch of science that studies the functions and activities of the nervous system, including nerves, the spinal cord and the brain. (तंत्रिका शरीरक्रिया विज्ञान)
◦ Example: Advances in neurophysiology have improved the treatment of epilepsy.

 

• Break the word into its roots: NEURO (nerve) + PHYSIO (nature, function) + LOGY (study of). Reading long scientific terms root by root is the safest method in spelling questions.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: "Nuerophysiology" — incorrect; the letters "e" and "u" in the first syllable have been interchanged. The root is neuro, as in neurology, neuron, neurotic.

 

• Option 3: "Neurophisiology" — incorrect; the root is "physio" (with ph and y), as in physics and physiotherapy.

 

• Option 4: "Neurophysiollogy" — incorrect; the suffix is "-logy" with a single "l".

 

NOTE

 

• Related terms worth remembering: neurology (study of nervous-system disorders), physiology (study of bodily functions), pathology (study of disease) and etymology (study of word origins).

question:
Choose the correct one-word substitute for the given expression.

 

'A supposed remedy that will cure all diseases and solve all problems'
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Panacea.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A panacea is a single remedy believed to cure every disease or settle every difficulty — a universal cure-all. (रामबाण औषधि)
◦ Example: Higher spending is no panacea for a badly designed scheme.

 

• The word comes from Greek pan (all) + akos (remedy). The same prefix pan- (all) appears in pandemic (affecting all people), panorama (a view of everything around) and pantheism.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Placebo (छद्म औषधि): a harmless substance given in place of a real medicine, chiefly to satisfy the patient or to serve as a control in a trial.

 

• Option 2: Antidote (मारक औषधि): a medicine that counteracts a specific poison — not a universal cure.

 

• Option 3: Palliative (उपशामक): something that relieves the symptoms without curing the underlying disease.

 

NOTE

 

• Related one-word substitutes tested by SSC: Elixir (a preparation supposed to prolong life indefinitely), Prophylactic (something that prevents disease), Sedative (something that calms) and Narcotic (a drug that induces sleep or stupor).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

He worked through the night lest he ___ miss the deadline set by the department.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. should.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The conjunction "lest" (meaning for fear that, in case) is always followed by "should" + the base form of the verb, irrespective of the tense of the main clause.

◦ Structure: … lest + subject + should + V1
◦ Example: Speak softly lest the child should wake up.

 

• "Lest" already carries a negative sense ("so that … not"), so it is never used with "not". Writing lest he should not miss would be a double negative and therefore wrong.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: would — not used after lest in standard grammar.

 

• Option 3: will — lest never takes a plain future auxiliary.

 

• Option 4: can — expresses ability or permission, which the sentence does not require.

 

NOTE

 

• Other conjunctions with fixed follow-ups: "unless" and "until" are never used with not; "scarcely/hardly" take when; "no sooner" takes than; "as if / as though" take were for unreal situations.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

The tribunal delivered its verdict on Monday, by ___ time the appellant had already withdrawn the petition.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. which.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "By which time" is a fixed relative expression used to link a later clause to a point of time already mentioned. It means "and by that time".

◦ Example: The results were declared in June, by which time most candidates had joined coaching classes.

 

• The relative pronoun "which" is the only one that can follow a preposition and then be linked to the noun time. The preposition placed before the relative — by which, at which, in which, for which — is the formal written pattern SSC prefers.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: that — "that" can never follow a preposition. We say the day on which, never the day on that.

 

• Option 2: what — used only when no antecedent noun is present (I know what he wants); here the antecedent Monday is already given.

 

• Option 4: whose — shows possession and is used mainly for persons; it does not fit after by.

 

NOTE

 

• Remember: which/whom may follow a preposition; that may not. Also, that is not used after a comma in a non-defining clause, which is another reason Option 1 fails here.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

Only a sustained public campaign can ___ the deep-rooted prejudice that the community still faces.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. eradicate.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Eradicate" means to destroy or remove something completely, to root out. It is the natural verb to use with deep-rooted things such as prejudice, poverty, corruption and disease. (जड़ से मिटाना)
◦ Example: India was declared free of polio after a campaign to eradicate the disease.

 

• The word comes from Latin e- (out) + radix (root) — literally "to pull out by the roots", which is exactly the image the sentence's phrase deep-rooted calls for.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: abrogate (निरस्त करना): to repeal or annul a law, treaty or agreement formally. A prejudice cannot be abrogated.

 

• Option 2: evacuate (खाली करना): to remove people from a place of danger.

 

• Option 3: abdicate (त्याग करना): to give up a throne, office or responsibility.

 

NOTE

 

• In such vocabulary-filler questions, look for the collocation clue planted in the sentence. Here the phrase "deep-rooted" points directly at the root-based verb eradicate.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

One of the most persistent problems (1)/ that the department have faced (2)/ over the last decade (3)/ remains unresolved. (4)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (2).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Inside the relative clause the subject is "the department", a singular collective noun, so the verb must be "has faced", not "have faced".

◦ Corrected sentence: One of the most persistent problems that the department has faced over the last decade remains unresolved.

 

• The nearby plural "problems" is a deliberate trap. It is the object of the clause, not its subject, so it cannot control the verb.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (1) is correct — "One of the + plural noun" is the standard structure (one of the problems, not one of the problem).

 

• Part (3) is correct — "over the last decade" is a well-formed adverbial of time.

 

• Part (4) is correct — the main subject is "One", which is singular, so "remains" is right.

 

NOTE

 

• Distinguish the two structures carefully:
◦ One of the + plural noun + singular verb → One of the boys is absent.
◦ One of those + plural noun + who + plural verb → He is one of those boys who are always late.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The report concedes that the guidelines, though comprehensive in scope, (1)/ may not be enforceable in practice (2)/ unless every state government (3)/ agree to adopt them without amendment. (4)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. (4).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The subject of part (4) is "every state government". The determiner "every" always makes a subject singular, so the verb must be "agrees", not "agree".

◦ Corrected sentence: … unless every state government agrees to adopt them without amendment.

 

• The rule holds even when every joins two nouns: "Every boy and every girl was present." The same applies to each, either, neither, everyone, somebody and nobody, all of which take singular verbs.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (1) is correct — the concessive phrase though comprehensive in scope is properly enclosed within commas.

 

• Part (2) is correct — "may not be enforceable" rightly uses the base form after the modal may.

 

• Part (3) is correct — "unless" already carries a negative sense and is correctly used here without not.

 

NOTE

 

• In long SSC sentences the verb is often separated from its true subject by several clauses. Locate the immediate subject of each numbered part and test agreement part by part.

question:
Change the following sentence from active voice to passive voice.

 

The archaeologists have unearthed several terracotta seals at the site.
option_1: Several terracotta seals were unearthed by the archaeologists at the site.
option_2: Several terracotta seals have been unearthed by the archaeologists at the site.
option_3: Several terracotta seals had been unearthed by the archaeologists at the site.
option_4: Several terracotta seals are being unearthed by the archaeologists at the site.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Several terracotta seals have been unearthed by the archaeologists at the site.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The given sentence is in the Present Perfect Tense — structure: Subject + have/has + V3.

 

• The passive of the present perfect is formed as: Object + have/has been + V3 + by + Subject.

◦ Active: The archaeologists have unearthed several terracotta seals.
◦ Passive: Several terracotta seals have been unearthed by the archaeologists.

 

• The auxiliary agrees with the new subject: seals is plural, so "have been" is used, not "has been".

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 uses "were unearthed" — the passive of the simple past, which loses the present-perfect link with the present.

 

• Option 3 uses "had been unearthed" — the passive of the past perfect, wrongly pushing the action further back in time.

 

• Option 4 uses "are being unearthed" — the passive of the present continuous, which makes the action ongoing rather than completed.

 

NOTE

 

• Passive forms of the perfect group: Present Perfect → has/have been + V3; Past Perfect → had been + V3; Future Perfect → will have been + V3. The perfect continuous tenses have no passive form in ordinary use.

question:
Convert the sentence given below from its passive voice structure to an active voice structure.

 

The prizes were being distributed by the chief guest when the lights went out.
option_1: The chief guest distributed the prizes when the lights went out.
option_2: The chief guest had distributed the prizes when the lights went out.
option_3: The chief guest was distributing the prizes when the lights went out.
option_4: The prizes distributed by the chief guest when the lights went out.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. The chief guest was distributing the prizes when the lights went out.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The given sentence is in the Past Continuous Passive — structure: was/were being + V3.

 

• Its active counterpart is the Past Continuous Active — structure: was/were + V-ing.

◦ Passive: The prizes were being distributed by the chief guest.
◦ Active: The chief guest was distributing the prizes.

 

• In the conversion the agent after "by" becomes the subject, the original subject becomes the object, and the continuous aspect must be preserved — the action was still in progress when the lights went out.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 uses the simple past "distributed", which presents the action as complete and loses the sense of interruption.

 

• Option 2 uses the past perfect, which wrongly places the distribution before the lights went out.

 

• Option 4 has no finite verb at all and is therefore not a complete sentence.

 

NOTE

 

• The word "when" joined to a continuous clause is the standard signal of an interrupted action: the longer action takes the continuous tense and the interrupting one takes the simple past.

question:
Select the sentence that contains the homophone of the highlighted word.

 

The advocate offered sound counsel to the young litigant.
option_1: The counsel for the defence rose to address the bench.
option_2: She sought the counsel of her elders before deciding.
option_3: The municipal council approved the budget unanimously.
option_4: His counsel on the matter proved invaluable.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. The municipal council approved the budget unanimously.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A homophone is a word that sounds the same as another but is spelt differently and carries a different meaning. (समोच्चारित किंतु भिन्न वर्तनी वाला शब्द)

 

• Counsel means advice, or a lawyer conducting a case. It can be a noun or a verb.
• Council means an assembly or governing body — a municipal council, a village council, a students' council. It is a noun only. The two are pronounced alike, so "council" is the homophone required here.

◦ Example: The council meets on the first Monday of every month.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Options 1, 2 and 4 all reuse the same spelling "counsel" in its different senses — a lawyer in Option 1, advice in Options 2 and 4. Same spelling with different meanings makes them homonyms, not homophones.

 

NOTE

 

• Memory aid: a council is a committee; counsel is advise or a solicitor.

 

• Other homophone pairs repeatedly asked in SSC: principal/principle, stationary/stationery, complement/compliment, cite/site/sight, eminent/imminent, alter/altar and draught/draft.

question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:

 

For much of the last century the disappearance of traditional crafts was treated as an unavoidable cost of progress. Hand-thrown pottery, hand-loomed cloth and hand-beaten metalwork could not compete with factory goods on either price or speed, and the workshops that produced them closed one after another. The argument seemed unanswerable: if a machine can shape in seconds a bowl that a potter needs an hour to make, sentiment alone cannot justify the potter's survival.

 

Yet the argument overlooks what is actually lost. A craft is not merely a method of manufacture; it is a body of knowledge held in the hands rather than in books — how a particular clay behaves in humid weather, which dye takes to which fibre, when a joint has been tightened enough. Such knowledge passes on only through long apprenticeship, and once a generation of practitioners dies without successors it cannot be recovered from museum specimens or written records. The loss is therefore permanent in a way that the closure of a factory is not.

 

Nor is the economic case as settled as it appears. Craft production is labour-intensive precisely where labour is abundant, it uses local materials, and it leaves earnings within the region instead of remitting them elsewhere. What it lacks is not demand but design, credit and access to distant markets — deficiencies that are administrative rather than inherent. Wherever cooperatives have supplied these three things, weavers and metalworkers have found buyers willing to pay a premium for objects that carry the marks of a particular hand.

 

The choice, then, was never simply between the loom and the machine. It was between treating a craft as an obsolete industry and treating it as a living archive that happens to earn its keep.

 

According to the passage, why is the loss of a craft permanent in a way that the closure of a factory is not?
option_1: Because factories can always be rebuilt with foreign investment
option_2: Because craft knowledge passes on only through apprenticeship and cannot be recovered from records
option_3: Because museums refuse to preserve handmade objects
option_4: Because the raw materials used by craftsmen are no longer available
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Because craft knowledge passes on only through apprenticeship and cannot be recovered from records.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The second paragraph states the reason directly: such knowledge passes on only through long apprenticeship, and once a generation of practitioners dies without successors it cannot be recovered from museum specimens or written records.

 

• The author's point is that a factory's machinery and methods are documented and reproducible, whereas a craft's knowledge lives in the practitioners themselves. That is what makes the loss irreversible.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 introduces foreign investment, a point the passage never raises.

 

• Option 3 contradicts the passage, which mentions museum specimens as existing but insufficient — not as refused.

 

• Option 4 is ruled out by the third paragraph, which says craft production uses local materials.

 

NOTE

 

• For reason-based questions, look for the sentence containing "therefore", "because", "since" or "thus". Here the word "therefore" in the last line of paragraph two marks the answer.

What does the author mean by "a body of knowledge held in the hands rather than in books"?
option_1: Knowledge that craftsmen deliberately keep secret from outsiders
option_2: Manual labour that requires no thought at all
option_3: Information carefully recorded in workshop registers
option_4: Practical skill learnt by doing, which cannot be fully written down
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Practical skill learnt by doing, which cannot be fully written down.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The phrase contrasts hands with books — that is, practical, physical skill as against written or theoretical learning.

 

• The examples the author gives immediately afterwards confirm this: knowing how a particular clay behaves in humid weather, which dye takes to which fibre, and when a joint has been tightened enough. These are judgements acquired only through repeated practice.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 wrongly introduces secrecy; the passage says such knowledge is hard to transmit, not deliberately hidden.

 

• Option 2 reverses the author's argument — the whole point is that craft work involves fine judgement, not thoughtless labour.

 

• Option 3 contradicts the phrase itself, which sets this knowledge against written records.

 

NOTE

 

• For figurative-expression questions, identify the contrast the phrase is built on (here hands versus books) and then check the examples that follow it — the author almost always illustrates the phrase in the next sentence.

According to the passage, what do craft industries actually lack?
option_1: Design, credit and access to distant markets
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Design, credit and access to distant markets.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The third paragraph states it plainly: what craft production lacks is not demand but design, credit and access to distant markets.

 

• The author adds that these deficiencies are administrative rather than inherent — that is, they arise from how the sector is organised and financed, not from any weakness in the craft itself. This is the basis of the author's argument that the economic case against crafts is not settled.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

• Option 2 is explicitly denied — the passage says the problem is "not demand".

 

• Option 3 is contradicted by paragraph two, which treats the practitioners' skill as the sector's central asset.

 

• Option 4 is contradicted by the statement that craft production uses local materials.

 

NOTE

 

• Watch for the construction "not X but Y" in comprehension passages. SSC very often builds one option out of X (the rejected item) to trap candidates who read only half the sentence.

option_2: Higher import duties on foreign textiles
option_3: Cooperatives that supplied design, credit and market access
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Cooperatives that supplied design, credit and market access.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The passage states that wherever cooperatives have supplied these three things, weavers and metalworkers have found buyers willing to pay a premium for objects carrying the marks of a particular hand.

 

• "These three things" refers back to the deficiencies named in the previous sentence — design, credit and access to distant markets. Reading the pronoun back to its antecedent is essential here.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Options 1 and 2 propose protectionist measures — bans and duties — which the passage nowhere recommends.

 

• Option 4 credits corporate advertising, whereas the passage credits cooperatives.

 

NOTE

 

• Options that sound like sensible real-world policy but are absent from the passage are the commonest SSC distractors. The answer must be traceable to a specific line of the text.

question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:

 

For much of the last century the disappearance of traditional crafts was treated as an unavoidable cost of progress. Hand-thrown pottery, hand-loomed cloth and hand-beaten metalwork could not compete with factory goods on either price or speed, and the workshops that produced them closed one after another. The argument seemed unanswerable: if a machine can shape in seconds a bowl that a potter needs an hour to make, sentiment alone cannot justify the potter's survival.

 

Yet the argument overlooks what is actually lost. A craft is not merely a method of manufacture; it is a body of knowledge held in the hands rather than in books — how a particular clay behaves in humid weather, which dye takes to which fibre, when a joint has been tightened enough. Such knowledge passes on only through long apprenticeship, and once a generation of practitioners dies without successors it cannot be recovered from museum specimens or written records. The loss is therefore permanent in a way that the closure of a factory is not.

 

Nor is the economic case as settled as it appears. Craft production is labour-intensive precisely where labour is abundant, it uses local materials, and it leaves earnings within the region instead of remitting them elsewhere. What it lacks is not demand but design, credit and access to distant markets — deficiencies that are administrative rather than inherent. Wherever cooperatives have supplied these three things, weavers and metalworkers have found buyers willing to pay a premium for objects that carry the marks of a particular hand.

 

The choice, then, was never simply between the loom and the machine. It was between treating a craft as an obsolete industry and treating it as a living archive that happens to earn its keep.

 

Which statement best expresses the author's final position?
option_1: Machine production should be abandoned in favour of handwork
option_2: A craft should be treated as a living archive that also earns its keep, not as an obsolete industry
option_3: Crafts survive today only because of public sentiment
option_4: Museums are the most suitable home for traditional crafts
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. A craft should be treated as a living archive that also earns its keep, not as an obsolete industry.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The closing paragraph frames the real choice: not between the loom and the machine, but between treating a craft as an obsolete industry and treating it as a living archive that happens to earn its keep.

 

• The phrase "living archive" captures the author's twin claim — a craft preserves knowledge (archive) and is still economically active (living). Option 2 reproduces both halves of that idea.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 overstates the case; the author never calls for machines to be given up.

 

• Option 3 is the argument the author is refuting — the opening paragraph presents sentiment as an insufficient defence, and the rest of the passage supplies better ones.

 

• Option 4 confines crafts to museums, which contradicts the word "living".

 

NOTE

 

• Questions on the author's view, tone or conclusion are almost always answered by the final two sentences of an argumentative passage. Read them with special care.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

The advisory board comprises of five members from each participating state.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. comprises five members.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The verb "comprise" means "to consist of" or "to be made up of". Since the sense of of is already contained in the verb, it is never followed by the preposition "of". Writing comprises of is a redundancy.

◦ Corrected sentence: The advisory board comprises five members from each participating state.

 

• The whole contains the parts: The board comprises five members. If you wish to move from parts to whole, use "constitute" or "compose": Five members constitute the board / The board is composed of five members.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 repeats the original error — the redundant "of".

 

• Option 3: "is comprised five members" is doubly wrong — the passive form would need of, and the active comprises is the preferred usage in any case.

 

• Option 4 keeps the redundant of and also uses the plural verb "comprise" with the singular subject board.

 

NOTE

 

• Other verbs that take no preposition in standard usage: discuss (not discuss about), order, request, resemble, accompany, emphasise (not emphasise on), investigate and reach (not reach at).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

He is one of those officers who is never satisfied with routine explanations.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. are never satisfied.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In the structure "one of those + plural noun + who", the relative pronoun "who" refers to the plural noun, not to "one". The verb in the relative clause must therefore be plural.

◦ Corrected sentence: He is one of those officers who are never satisfied with routine explanations.

 

• Test it by rearranging: Of those officers who are never satisfied, he is one. The plural verb becomes obvious.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Options 1 and 2 use singular verbs, wrongly linking who to "one" instead of "officers".

 

• Option 3: "has never satisfied" changes the meaning altogether — it turns the officers into the ones doing the satisfying rather than being satisfied.

 

NOTE

 

• Contrast the two structures carefully:
◦ One of the + plural noun + singular verb → One of the officers is on leave.
◦ One of those + plural noun + who + plural verb → He is one of those officers who are never satisfied.

 

• If "the only" is added, the verb turns singular again: He is the only one of those officers who is never satisfied.

question:
A sentence is provided in direct speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding indirect speech.

 

Ravi said, "I am writing the departmental examination tomorrow."
option_1: Ravi said that he is writing the departmental examination tomorrow.
option_2: Ravi said that he was writing the departmental examination tomorrow.
option_3: Ravi said that he was writing the departmental examination the next day.
option_4: Ravi said that he had written the departmental examination the next day.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Ravi said that he was writing the departmental examination the next day.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The reporting verb "said" is in the past tense, so the reported speech must be backshifted by one degree:

◦ Tense: Present Continuous (am writing) → Past Continuous (was writing).
◦ Pronoun: I → he, matching the subject of the reporting clause.
◦ Time expression: tomorrow → the next day / the following day.

 

• Applying all three changes together gives Option 3.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 fails to backshift the tense at all and keeps tomorrow unchanged.

 

• Option 2 backshifts the tense correctly but leaves "tomorrow" unchanged — the commonest trap in narration questions.

 

• Option 4 wrongly uses the past perfect "had written", which places a future action in the past.

 

NOTE

 

• Standard time-word changes: now → then; today → that day; tomorrow → the next day; yesterday → the previous day; last night → the previous night; next week → the following week; here → there; this → that; ago → before.

question:
A sentence is provided in indirect speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding direct speech.

 

He asked me whether I had received the letter.
option_1: "Have you received the letter?" he asked me.
option_2: "Did you receive the letter?" he asked me.
option_3: "Had you received the letter?" he asked me.
option_4: "You have received the letter," he asked me.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. "Have you received the letter?" he asked me.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The sentence is an interrogative reported with "asked … whether". Converting it back to direct speech requires the reverse of the usual rules:

◦ Drop the conjunction whether/if.
◦ Restore the question order — auxiliary before subject — and end with a question mark.
◦ Undo the backshift: had received → have received.
◦ Change the pronoun back: I → you (the listener).

 

• This produces: "Have you received the letter?" he asked me.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 uses the simple past "Did you receive", whose indirect form would be asked whether I had received as well — but the perfect form is the closer and standard reversal of had received.

 

• Option 3 keeps the past perfect unchanged, which cannot appear in the original spoken question.

 

• Option 4 is an assertive sentence with a full stop, so it cannot follow the reporting verb asked.

 

NOTE

 

• Rules for questions in narration: Yes/No questions take if / whether; Wh- questions retain the question word; the reporting verb changes to asked, enquired or demanded; and the question mark disappears in indirect speech.

question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

 

S1. The tea stall at the bus stand had been Ramu's whole world for eleven years.

 

A. He began keeping a battered notebook under the counter to copy the letters out.

 

B. A retired schoolmaster who came every evening noticed the notebook and offered to teach him after closing hours.

 

C. Customers often left their newspapers behind, and he would stare at headlines he could not read.

 

D. Within two years he was reading those same newspapers aloud to the other stall owners.

 

S2. He now runs an evening literacy class for the porters at the same bus stand.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. C-A-B-D.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct sequence is S1 – C – A – B – D – S2. The paragraph follows a situation → first step → help → outcome → present position order.

 

• S1 sets the situation — the tea stall has been Ramu's world for eleven years.

◦ C introduces the problem: the abandoned newspapers and headlines he could not read. It must come first because it is the only sentence that explains what the "letters" in A refer to.
◦ A is his first step — copying those letters into a notebook.
◦ B must follow A, since the schoolmaster "noticed the notebook", an object that exists only after A.
◦ D gives the outcome — he is now reading "those same newspapers", which points back to C and rounds off the episode before S2.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (A-C-B-D) begins with the notebook before the newspapers have been mentioned, leaving "the letters" without an antecedent.

 

• Option 2 (C-B-A-D) lets the schoolmaster notice a notebook that has not yet been started.

 

• Option 4 (B-A-C-D) opens with the schoolmaster, so both the notebook and the newspapers appear only after they have been referred to.

 

NOTE

 

• The strongest tool in rearrangement is the object-introduction test: a thing must be introduced before it can be referred to with the, those or same. Here "the notebook" in B and "those same newspapers" in D fix the whole order by themselves.

question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

 

S1. Few claims about human engineering have been repeated as confidently as the one about the Great Wall of China.

 

A. Astronauts who have actually orbited the earth report that they can see no such thing.

 

B. Generations of textbooks asserted that it was the only man-made structure visible from space.

 

C. The wall, though immensely long, is narrow and built of materials that blend into the surrounding terrain.

 

D. The claim, it turns out, had been circulating in print long before anyone had been to space at all.

 

S2. It survives today chiefly as a reminder of how rarely a striking statement is checked before being repeated.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. B-A-C-D.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct sequence is S1 – B – A – C – D – S2. The paragraph moves from claim → contradiction → explanation → origin → verdict.

 

• S1 announces that a much-repeated claim is about to be examined.

◦ B states what the claim actually was — that the wall is the only man-made structure visible from space. S1 mentions "the one about the Great Wall" without spelling it out, so B must follow immediately.
◦ A supplies the contradiction — astronauts report seeing no such thing.
◦ C explains why they cannot: the wall is narrow and blends into the terrain.
◦ D traces the claim's origin, showing it predates spaceflight, which leads directly into the verdict in S2.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (A-B-D-C) denies the claim before it has been stated.

 

• Option 3 (B-C-A-D) gives the explanation before the reader learns that the claim is false, so "no such thing" in A loses its force.

 

• Option 4 (C-B-A-D) opens with a physical description of a wall that has not yet been discussed in detail.

 

NOTE

 

• In an argument-and-rebuttal paragraph the order is almost always: statement of the claim → evidence against it → explanation → conclusion. Identify which sentence states the claim, and the rest usually falls into place.
